cells.tense: You can feel which parts of your life are finished, and you are letting them finish.
cells.ask: Say out loud to one person that something is over. Name only that. Then let the next thing arrive on its own schedule. The naming is the whole act — nothing has to follow it.
cells.core:
You can feel the difference between what's finished and what's merely hard. That's why endings land cleanly with you — you let a thing be over when it's over, and something in you trusts that the next thing is already moving. It's not that you don't grieve. You grieve and you keep the door open anyway.

What you have is doing what it's made for: clearing room, honoring what was, and letting a beginning stay small until it's ready. What this feeds next is fair dealing — you can give and take with people because you're not secretly negotiating with something that's ended. Hold the clearing loosely, though. The skill here is timing, not resolve, and the room you've made stays yours only if you don't start defending it.
cells.sheetLine: You can end a thing cleanly and trust what comes next.
cells.verb: clearing what is finished so what is coming can enter
cells.place: at the threshold where one thing ends and the next has not yet crossed

cells.tense: You are living past this moment, opening a door before the hinge has had a chance to turn.
cells.ask: Leave one unfinished thing alone for a week. Put it where you can see it and don't touch it or decide about it. If it still needs to end after the week, end it then — after, not during.
cells.core:
Endings come to you faster than they need to. A thing gets useful, meaningful, or real, and some part of you is already packing it up — you call it clearing, you call it growth, and underneath it's the bracing against being caught off guard. So nothing gets to live long enough to show you what it is.

The room keeps getting emptied and nothing new has time to arrive, because you keep the threshold busy. The endings aren't wrong — they're early. What's waiting is not another liberation; it's finding out what connection feels like when you stay for it, including the parts you'd rather preempt. Let one thing sit, and stay in the room with it. The staying is the work.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending things early and calling it being ready.
cells.verb: clearing what is finished so what is coming can enter

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that is already behind you, holding the frame as if it were still shut.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been keeping out of loyalty and take one small step out of it — one call, one box, one tie cut. Notice what's still there afterward. The step is the whole act; do less if less is what's true.
cells.core:
Something you're holding onto is no longer holding you. You call it loyalty — that's the honest name for it — and the loyalty is real, but it's stopped being toward anything alive. The room around you hasn't caught up with what you already sense, so the days feel like staying when they could feel like leaving.

What's starved isn't courage. It's the pull of a direction you actually feel. You don't need a bigger ending; you need one small move with feeling behind it, and the movement itself will pull the threshold back into your life. Don't push yourself toward feeling — push toward one step and let the feeling show up in the doing. What's coming isn't asking you to like the ending. Only to be at it.
cells.sheetLine: The thing you're keeping is already gone, and you're keeping it anyway.

cells.tense: Something in you is ending right now, and you are speaking about it as though nothing is.
cells.ask: Write down one thing in your life you've been describing as temporary. Just the sentence, in your own hand. Reread it tomorrow. No decision is required from you today.
cells.core:
You describe the erosion as conditions. Things loosen, people drift, plans stop holding, and you'll say it's a phase, or a busy stretch, or that's just how it goes — while the ground under all of it is genuinely moving. You aren't lying to anyone. The naming has simply stayed inside your head.

Being the one who names what's ending is a form of authority — not control, just saying what's true before deciding anything about it. That's the smaller, older skill the moment is asking you to reach back for: name the thing, and the naming gives you ground. Once it has a name, you can build with it or end it. Right now nothing is being built, because the change is still going unnamed. Say the sentence once and let it stand.
cells.sheetLine: Something in you is ending and you're still calling it a phase.

attempts.check: The record gives me Transformation as necessary endings and clearing, but nothing says what is actually ending in this person's life; every cell must stay with the mechanism of ending and arriving and leave the content to them, and Too Little must not guess at any past room or loss. The reader could reasonably say the ending I'm pointing at isn't the one they're in — so each cell is written so that a wrong guess still leaves a usable act, a step they can take whatever the ending turns out to be. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line that reads as wisdom about endings in general; the ending is theirs to name, and the reading only says what capacity is doing the naming. The asks all survive being wrong because they are acts toward a welcoming or a leaving, not verdicts about what the person's life is doing.
